scenes.tts: The first film showed how Toll-like receptors free NF kappa B within minutes. Once that powerful inflammatory alarm fires, why does it not kill the cell or wreck the body? Follow what happens right on DNA.
scenes.caption: The first film showed how Toll-like receptors free NF-κB within minutes. Once that powerful inflammatory alarm fires, why does it not kill the cell or wreck the body? Follow what happens right on DNA.
scenes.visual: Opens directly where the first film ended, reusing the exact macrophage cross-section and colour map: emerald NF-κB sits on glowing purple DNA inside the nucleus. Bright amber alarm pulses radiate upward while a coral warning halo flickers gently at the cell border. Label: 'Alarm ON: what stops it?'
scenes.narration: The first film showed how Toll-like receptors free NF-κB within minutes. Once that powerful inflammatory alarm fires, why does it not kill the cell or wreck the body? Follow what happens right on DNA.

scenes.visual: The macrophage dims gently while the title 'Why the Alarm Needs Brakes' appears cleanly in white at top center and fades out as the purple DNA keeps pulsing.

scenes.tts: The answer starts right on that DNA. Along with inflammatory genes, emerald NF kappa B turns on two brakes of its own. First, it makes fresh coral I kappa B alpha. That new inhibitor enters the nucleus, lifts the switch off DNA, and pulls it outside.
scenes.caption: The answer starts right on that DNA. Along with inflammatory genes, emerald NF-κB turns on two brakes of its own. First, it makes fresh coral IκBα. That new inhibitor enters the nucleus, lifts the switch off DNA, and pulls it outside.
scenes.visual: From the purple DNA, a glowing coral ribbon emerges and folds into a fresh coral clamp labelled 'New IκBα'. The coral clamp enters the purple nucleus, clasps emerald NF-κB off the DNA, and ferries it back out into the cytosol.
scenes.narration: The answer starts right on that DNA. Along with inflammatory genes, emerald NF-κB turns on two brakes of its own. First, it makes fresh coral IκBα. That new inhibitor enters the nucleus, lifts the switch off DNA, and pulls it outside.

scenes.tts: Second, it turns on an enzyme called A20. A20 strips the sky-blue lysine 63 scaffold chains upstream, shutting the relay off near its source. New I kappa B alpha takes time to make, so this negative feedback arrives late. Under a lasting stimulus, nuclear NF kappa B therefore rises and falls in waves.
scenes.caption: Second, it turns on an enzyme called A20. A20 strips the sky-blue lysine-63 scaffold chains upstream, shutting the relay off near its source. New IκBα takes time to make, so this negative feedback arrives late. Under a lasting stimulus, nuclear NF-κB therefore rises and falls in waves.
scenes.visual: A coral scissor icon labelled 'A20' glides up to the sky-blue K63 scaffold chain in the cytosol and snips it apart, dimming teal IKK. On the right half of the frame, an animated curve labelled 'Nuclear NF-κB (schematic)' traces smooth rising and falling waves over time.

New IκBα takes time to make, so this negative feedback arrives late. Under a lasting stimulus, nuclear NF-κB therefore rises and falls in waves.

scenes.tts: NF kappa B also spreads the alarm. One target gene encodes tumor necrosis factor, or TNF, a secreted signaling protein called a cytokine. Amber TNF binds TNF receptor 1 on the same cell and its neighbors. That single receptor sends two opposite messages at once: die, and stay alive.
scenes.caption: NF-κB also spreads the alarm. One target gene encodes tumor necrosis factor, or TNF, a secreted signaling protein called a cytokine. Amber TNF binds TNF receptor 1 on the same cell and its neighbors. That single receptor sends two opposite messages at once: die, and stay alive.
scenes.visual: The macrophage releases glowing amber TNF particles that land on a teal receptor labelled 'TNF receptor 1' on its own surface and on a neighboring cell. Inside the neighbor, the signal forks into two moving arrows: a coral arrow toward a death icon ('Die') and an emerald arrow toward NF-κB ('Stay alive').
scenes.narration: NF-κB also spreads the alarm. One target gene encodes tumor necrosis factor, or TNF, a secreted signaling protein called a cytokine. Amber TNF binds TNF receptor 1 on the same cell and its neighbors. That single receptor sends two opposite messages at once: die, and stay alive.

scenes.tts: Normally, stay alive wins. First, an immediate brake right at the receptor holds the death machinery back without new genes. Then NF kappa B turns on survival genes that shield the cell. Block that survival arm and the same TNF kills the cell. That is why this is called the anti-death, death pathway.
scenes.caption: Normally, stay alive wins. First, an immediate brake right at the receptor holds the death machinery back without new genes. Then NF-κB turns on survival genes that shield the cell. Block that survival arm and the same TNF kills the cell. That is why this is called the anti-death, death pathway.
scenes.visual: Inside the neighbor cell, a teal clamp halts the coral death arrow right at the receptor ('Receptor checkpoint'), and emerald NF-κB enters the nucleus to raise a glowing emerald shield ('Survival genes') blocking the coral arrow. A split-frame contrast then locks emerald NF-κB behind an unbreakable coral IκB clamp: the shield vanishes, and the coral death arrow fragments the cell.
scenes.narration: Normally, stay alive wins. First, an immediate brake right at the receptor holds the death machinery back without new genes. Then NF-κB turns on survival genes that shield the cell. Block that survival arm and the same TNF kills the cell. That is why this is called the anti-death, death pathway.

scenes.tts: Now zoom out and predict. Normal mice collapse into shock from a heavy dose of purified bacterial endotoxin. Mice lacking working TLR4 shrug off that exact same dose. How do those endotoxin-resistant mice fare when they meet live Gram-negative bacteria?
scenes.caption: Now zoom out and predict. Normal mice collapse into shock from a heavy dose of purified bacterial endotoxin. Mice lacking working TLR4 shrug off that exact same dose. How do those endotoxin-resistant mice fare when they meet live Gram-negative bacteria?
scenes.visual: Frame shifts cleanly to a two-panel schematic comparison of normal and TLR4-mutant mice. Left panel ('Purified endotoxin'): normal mouse glows coral-red ('Shock') while TLR4-mutant mouse stays steady ('No shock'). Right panel ('Live bacteria'): question card overlays the mutant mouse: 'TLR4-mutant mice meet live bacteria: better or worse off?'
scenes.narration: Now zoom out and predict. Normal mice collapse into shock from a heavy dose of purified bacterial endotoxin. Mice lacking working TLR4 shrug off that exact same dose. How do those endotoxin-resistant mice fare when they meet live Gram-negative bacteria?

scenes.visual: Thinking pause: the question 'TLR4-mutant mice meet live bacteria: better or worse off?' stays clearly on screen while a subtle progress bar fills slowly over 4.5 seconds and amber bacteria drift softly near the mutant mouse.

scenes.tts: Far worse off, because they never raise the early alarm. Live bacteria multiply faster and kill them far more easily. Humans show both failures too. Children born without working MyD88 or IRAK4 suffer repeated severe infections with pus-forming bacteria, often with little fever.
scenes.caption: Far worse off, because they never raise the early alarm. Live bacteria multiply faster and kill them far more easily. Humans show both failures too. Children born without working MyD88 or IRAK4 suffer repeated severe infections with pus-forming bacteria, often with little fever.
scenes.visual: The question clears to 'Worse off: no early alarm' as amber bacteria multiply around the mutant mouse. Below, a horizontal balance beam labelled 'Innate alarm balance (schematic)' tips left into coral ('Too little: MyD88 or IRAK4 loss').
scenes.narration: Far worse off, because they never raise the early alarm. Live bacteria multiply faster and kill them far more easily. Humans show both failures too. Children born without working MyD88 or IRAK4 suffer repeated severe infections with pus-forming bacteria, often with little fever.

scenes.tts: At the other extreme, endotoxin circulating in some infections triggers widespread TNF release, and septic shock can follow. Blood vessels widen and leak, blood pressure drops, and the host's own alarm injures organs. Human sepsis is more complex than endotoxin shock alone. Yet a modified endotoxin fragment, far less toxic, helps vaccines work.

scenes.visual: The balance beam tips right into coral ('Too much: septic shock') as leaking vessel icons pulse coral, then settles onto its glowing emerald center ('Controlled vaccine adjuvant') where a small amber dot sparks a brief, calm emerald pulse.

scenes.tts: Scope matters. TNF receptor 1 also has an immediate brake on death, and separate cytosolic sensors detect viral nucleic acids. Within canonical Toll-like receptor signaling, NF kappa B drives survival and brakes alongside inflammation, so defense usually spares the host.

scenes.visual: Wide schematic summary of the emerald center zone showing three glowing outputs emerging from NF-κB on purple DNA: 'Defense', 'Survival', and 'Brakes'. A quiet side note briefly reads 'Cytosolic alarms: next in text'. The scene fades smoothly to dark.

scenes.visual: Clean dark end card displaying one centered line only, with no smaller line underneath: 'NF-κB drives defense, survival and brakes, balancing protection against host injury.'
